questions.q: Why can comparing agents' raw average resolution times be unfair?
options: Averages cannot be computed per agent
Agents may receive different mixes of case priority, and some priorities take longer for everyone
Resolution time is not recorded on cases
All agents always receive identical cases
questions.explain: If one agent handles more slow, low-priority cases, their raw average will be higher even at team-average speed.

questions.q: Omar's mix is 12% High, 43% Medium and 45% Low, with team averages of 9.5, 34 and 61 hours. Roughly what is his expected average?
options: 9.5 hours
61 hours
34 hours
43 hours

questions.q: How do you reconcile a per-agent scorecard?
options: Check that agents' closed counts add up to the team total from your earlier reports
Ask each agent to confirm their own number
Remove the team row
Round every figure to zero decimals
questions.explain: 340 + 310 + 290 + 240 equals 1,180, the quarter's closed total. A mismatch signals a filter or ownership problem.

questions.q: Which data pitfall can hide cases from every agent's row in a report grouped by Case Owner?
options: Cases with a priority
Cases that are closed
Cases owned by a queue instead of a person
Cases created on weekends
questions.explain: Case Owner can be a queue, so unassigned or queue-owned cases appear under the queue's name rather than an agent's.

questions.q: What is the most responsible way to present agent performance data?
options: A public leaderboard ranked by one metric
As workload and coaching insight, with caveats and multiple metrics rather than a single ranking
Only the fastest agent's data
Without any context so it speaks for itself
questions.explain: Performance data affects people. Frame it around workload, mix, and support, and state what the data cannot show.
